newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SA WEEK AHEAD-S.AFRICAN JUNE M3, CPI SEEN DOWN.
newsitem.headline: SA WEEK AHEAD-S.AFRICAN JUNE M3, CPI SEEN DOWN.

text.p: * M3 seen lower on technical factors and fall in credit extension.
* Credit extension seen helped by high year-ago base, continuing recent year-on-year trend lower on the back of high interest rates and high consumer indebtedness.
* CPI seen down on lower petrol price and generally benign inflationary pressures. High year-ago base will also help. Food prices seen under pressure.
* Reserves to benefit from Yankee proceeds and foreign bond purchases, but offset by Reserve Bank intervention in forex market.
By Paul Richardson
South Africa's financial markets are braced for an avalanche of economic indicators next week, all of which should continue to point the way to lower interest rates, economists said on Friday.
Money supply growth, private sector credit extension growth and consumer inflation are all expected to have fallen in June, adding further ammunition to economists call for a cut in interest rates.
Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals' has stated in the past that he will not relax monetary policy until the three indicators have slowed.
The central bank will release June money supply and private sector credit extension data at 1500 GMT on Monday.
A Reuters consensus poll of economists forecast money supply growth would rise 14.4 percent year-on-year compared with a preliminary 15.4 percent increase in May.
Economists said the main reasons for the slowdown in money supply growth would be a high base in June last year coupled with a continuing slowdown in credit extension.
"Apart from the fact that we are expecting credit to come off, there are technical factors. M3 is basically coming off a high base," Nedcor chief economist Dennis Dykes said.
The consensus forecast for credit extension was for a 15.19 percent year-on-year rise from May's 16.57 percent.

Barnard Jacobs Mellet economist Chantal Friedman said credit extension was expected to rebound in the month from its low month-on-month increase of 0.2 percent in May as June was a seasonally high month.
"However, while we expect a higher month-on-month rate, the impact of high interest rates and high consumer debt should limit overall growth in this aggregate," she said.
"As with M3, a high base in June 1996 should result in a sharp fall in the year-on-year rate," she added
On Tuesday, Central Statistical Services releases June consumer inflation data at 0900 GMT, which economists expect to continue the trend of the last two months by falling further.

"Core inflation is ticking along very slowly at the moment and that combines with the arithmetic benefits that we have seen over the last two months figures of the base beginning to accelerate, which brings the year-on-year down a bit," said Econometrix economist Tony Twine.
Economists forecast June CPI would rise 9.1 percent year-on-year compared with May's 9.5 percent rise.
Friedman said the increase in consumer inflation would be limited by a sharp fall in petrol prices in the month.
"The only major quarterly survey in June is furniture and equipment, where prices appear to have been reasonably steady over the second quarter," she added.

Huysamer Stals economist Johan Rossouw said food prices were expected to have come under pressure from both the cold snap at the end of May and a rise in vegetable exports which would have reduced local supplies.
On Friday, the Reserve Bank will release July gold and foreign exchange reserves data at 1600 GMT.
Economists were loathe to forecast the indicator a week before month end, but said that indications were the figure would be sideways to higher.

Edey Rogers economist Hugo Klein said that he expected the proceeds of government's $250 million Yankee bond issue in June to be offset by Reserve Bank intervention in the foreign exchange market in the month.

Economists also noted that while foreigners had been net sellers of domestic bonds at one point in the month, the resumption of buying in the latter half of the month would have probably neutralised those outflows.
Reserves were expected to come in between 21.5 billion rand to 23.3 billion rand from 22.1 billion rand in June.
